title: AI drives Treasury shift to resilience
full_text:
Treasury has shifted its advice to give greater emphasis to economic resilience as the government faces difficult choices to protect the country from an onslaught of economic risks from conflict, advancing artificial intelligence and globally rising inflation, the treasury secretary has revealed.
While economic shocks were not new, the "unusually wide range of challenges" this year had shaken Treasury's world view. These challenges forced it to respond in new ways to mitigate the impact of great power competition, Jenny Wilkinson told the United States Studies Centre economic security forum in Sydney on Monday.
Australia had shown "remarkable resilience" during the 2008 global financial crisis, the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic and the 2022 energy shock from Russia's invasion of Ukraine, due to its flexible economy and the government's "fiscal space" to respond, "but these defences are no longer enough," she said.
"Economic security risks are rising owing to escalating geostrategic competition, rapid technological change, and the growing weaponisation of economic dependencies for strategic ends," Wilkinson said.
"In the past, our advice to government attached relatively little weight to the role of resilience and sovereign capability. We recognise that the world has changed. We're not abandoning our economic thinking, but we are applying it in a different context," she said.
"This changing landscape is creating difficult choices for government. As a nation, we've always sought to build resilience to shocks, but as the threats increase, so does the cost of insuring against them."
Wilkinson's speech centred on the Treasury's increasing focus on economic resilience - assisted by a new economic security unit that feeds intelligence insights into economic decision-making.
